title: What's New in Kotlin Jump
tagline: An extracted key is never a reserved word
summary: Extract to string resource names the key after the text of the literal. When that text is a keyword of the language, the key was one too, and the project stopped compiling.

highlights.title: A literal reading true no longer produces a key named true
highlights.description: The build tool writes the key as a field of the generated R class, so a Java keyword there is a syntax error, and a key named is cannot even be written in Kotlin without backticks.

sections.heading: Fixes
bullets: Measured on a real project: of 11786 literals, 85 produced a reserved key, across ten distinct words. The word true alone accounted for 34 of them, then null, false, native, default, class, else, super, is and package. None do now.
The rescue is the prefix the code already used for a name that starts with a digit, so there is one habit rather than two, and the result still has to be unique against the keys already declared.
The list covers the keywords of both languages, since the key is read from Java in the generated class and written from Kotlin at the call site.

sections.heading: Notes
bullets: Found by asking a simple question of every literal in the project: is the key this would generate a name the build can actually carry. The same sweep confirms the escaping fixed yesterday, with 10623 of 10624 template free literals coming back identical through the extraction.
